questions.prompt: Which set is the nonnegative orthant of \(\mathbb{R}^n\)?
questions.explanation: The nonnegative orthant is \(\{x: x_i \ge 0 \text{ for every } i\}\). The extra constraint that the coordinates sum to 1 cuts out the unit simplex. Length 1 is a sphere. A line is a one-dimensional affine set.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 260 200" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>shaded first quadrant</title><line x1="48" y1="168" x2="236" y2="168"/><polygon points="236,168 229.6,170.7 229.6,165.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="48" y1="180" x2="48" y2="24"/><polygon points="48,24 50.7,30.4 45.3,30.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="230" y="184" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x1</text><text x="56" y="20" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x2</text><rect x="48" y="48" width="150" height="120" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.10"/></svg>
questions.figure_alt: The closed first quadrant is shaded.
options: every nonnegative vector whose coordinates sum to 1
every vector whose coordinates are all at least zero

questions.prompt: How many vertices does the unit simplex \(\{x \ge 0: x_1+x_2+x_3 = 1\}\) in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) have?
questions.explanation: The vertices are the three standard basis vectors. Every other point of the simplex is a convex combination of those three, so it is not extreme. Counting the origin as well would describe a different simplex, the one defined by \(x \ge 0\) and \(x_1+x_2+x_3 \le 1\).
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 280 200" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>segment between axis intercepts</title><line x1="40" y1="168" x2="250" y2="168"/><polygon points="250,168 243.6,170.7 243.6,165.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="48" y1="184" x2="48" y2="22"/><polygon points="48,22 50.7,28.4 45.3,28.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="244" y="184" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x1</text><text x="56" y="18" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x2</text><line x1="188" y1="168" x2="48" y2="48" stroke-width="2.4"/><circle cx="188" cy="168" r="2.6" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="48" cy="48" r="2.6" fill="currentColor"/></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A segment joins a positive intercept on each axis.

questions.explanation: One nontrivial linear equation cuts the dimension by 1, which is a hyperplane. Two inequalities describe a wedge or a slab. A unit ball is curved. A space of matrices is not that flat subset of \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 280 200" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>line with one side shaded</title><line x1="36" y1="168" x2="250" y2="168"/><polygon points="250,168 243.6,170.7 243.6,165.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="48" y1="184" x2="48" y2="22"/><polygon points="48,22 50.7,28.4 45.3,28.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="244" y="184" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x1</text><text x="56" y="18" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x2</text><polygon points="70,150 210,40 250,40 250,170 70,170" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.15"/><line x1="60" y1="158" x2="220" y2="30" stroke-width="2.2"/></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A straight boundary, with one side of the plane shaded.
options: the solution set of two independent inequalities
the unit ball of any norm
the set of all \(m \times n\) matrices
the solution set of one linear equation \(a^T x = \beta\) with \(a \ne 0\)

questions.prompt: The closed line segment from \(a\) to \(b\) is
questions.explanation: The parameter \(t\) runs from 0 to 1, including the endpoints, so the set is closed and bounded. Every real \(t\) is the whole line. \(t \ge 0\) is the ray that starts at \(a\). Equal distance to \(a\) and \(b\) is the perpendicular bisector.

questions.figure_alt: A solid segment lies on a longer dashed line.

questions.prompt: What is the first coordinate of the midpoint of \((2, 8)\) and \((10, 0)\)?
questions.explanation: The midpoint is \(\frac12(2+10, 8+0) = (6, 4)\). The first coordinate is 6. The second coordinate is 4, and either endpoint alone would give 2 or 10.

questions.figure_alt: A solid segment lies on a longer dashed line.

questions.prompt: What is the sum of the coordinates of \((0.2, 0.5, 0.3)\)?
questions.explanation: \(0.2+0.5+0.3 = 1\). Together with the nonnegative coordinates, that sum is what places the point on the unit simplex. A sum of \(0.6\) would fall short of the plane, and a sum of \(2\) would overshoot it.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 280 200" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>segment between axis intercepts</title><line x1="40" y1="168" x2="250" y2="168"/><polygon points="250,168 243.6,170.7 243.6,165.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="48" y1="184" x2="48" y2="22"/><polygon points="48,22 50.7,28.4 45.3,28.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="244" y="184" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x1</text><text x="56" y="18" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x2</text><line x1="188" y1="168" x2="48" y2="48" stroke-width="2.4"/><circle cx="188" cy="168" r="2.6" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="48" cy="48" r="2.6" fill="currentColor"/></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A segment joins a positive intercept on each axis.

questions.prompt: What is the affine dimension of a hyperplane in \(\mathbb{R}^4\)?
questions.explanation: One independent linear equation reduces dimension by 1, so a hyperplane in \(\mathbb{R}^4\) has dimension 3. Dimension 4 would be the whole space. Dimension 1 would be a line, which needs three independent equations in \(\mathbb{R}^4\).

questions.figure_alt: A straight boundary, with one side of the plane shaded.

questions.prompt: A matrix in \(\mathbb{R}^{2 \times 3}\) describes a linear map
questions.explanation: Columns are the domain dimension and rows are the codomain dimension. A \(2 \times 3\) matrix sends a 3-vector to a 2-vector. Swapping those dimensions describes a \(3 \times 2\) matrix instead.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a 2 by 3 matrix</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">a   b   c</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">d   e   f</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A matrix with two rows and three columns.

questions.prompt: A point moves from \((0, 0)\) to \((5, 20)\) as the parameter \(t\) runs from 0 to 1. At \(t = 1/5\), what is its second coordinate?
questions.explanation: The point is \((1-t)\) times the start plus \(t\) times the end. At \(t = 1/5\) the second coordinate is \(20/5 = 4\). The first coordinate is 1. The parameter \(t = 4/5\) would land at second coordinate 16.

questions.explanation: A norm's closed unit ball is every vector whose norm is at most 1. The inequality is not strict, so the sphere is included. The set is curved, so it is not a hyperplane, and the coordinates of a unit vector need not sum to 1.

questions.prompt: The segment from \((0,0)\) to \((6,10)\) is the set of convex combinations of its endpoints. What is the second coordinate of the combination with weight \(1/2\) on \((6,10)\)?
questions.explanation: Weight \(1/2\) is the midpoint \((3, 5)\). The second coordinate is 5. Weight \(1\) would give 10, and the first coordinate of the midpoint is 3.

questions.prompt: A sublevel set of a scalar function \(f\) at height \(a\) is
questions.explanation: The sublevel set keeps every point whose value is at most \(a\). The equality \(f(x) = a\) is a level set, or contour. The domain is where \(f\) is defined, not where it is small. Only special functions have flat sublevel sets.
